Privacy-reviewed judgment extracts

Each block quote reproduces selected words from the court document. The Navigator supplies the context below each quotation. Identifying details and the full court documents are withheld where public access could compromise privacy.

Delhi High Court judgment on complaint screening and interim suspension

Delhi High Court · April 2026 · Paragraphs 56.2 and 57

The creation of a fact finding committee in order to determine whether a given complaint is to be sent to the ICC/Local Committee

Decision in context

The Court held that an employer cannot create a parallel fact-finding body to decide whether a POSH complaint should reach the statutory Internal or Local Committee. It recognised the employer’s power to suspend in the circumstances, set aside the stigmatic suspension order and gave the employer liberty to issue a fresh one.

Delhi High Court judgment on bias and constitution of a fresh Internal Committee

Delhi High Court · October 2026 · Paragraphs 37–39

do not disclose any real likelihood of bias
The present petition is, accordingly, dismissed

Decision in context

The Court dismissed the challenge to a freshly constituted Internal Committee. On the record, ordinary reporting relationships and attendance at a meeting did not establish a real likelihood of bias. The Court also accepted the written appeal procedure in the circumstances.

Delhi High Court judgment on identifying the Section 18 appellate authority

Delhi High Court · February 2026 · Paragraphs 8–10

the appeal against the impugned report would lie before the authority as designated in notification dated 04.05.2016

Decision in context

The Court applied the relevant Gazette notification to identify the appellate forum and allowed the petitioner 30 days to file, directing consideration on the merits without dismissal on limitation grounds.

Delhi High Court judgment on Local Committee jurisdiction and retaliatory discharge

Delhi High Court · August 2025 · Paragraphs 110–114

the LCC had jurisdiction to inquire into the Petitioner’s complaint
the termination of her services was vitiated by mala fides and non-compliance with the principles of natural justice

Decision in context

The Court held the Secretary to be the statutory employer on the governing framework, so the complaint belonged before the LC. It set aside the retaliatory discharge and the IC report issued without jurisdiction, and directed the complaint to proceed before the LC.

Supreme Court order on access to an inquiry report

Supreme Court of India · December 2024 · Signed order, pages 5–6

required to be given under Section 13 (1) to all the “concerned parties”
Petitioner is definitely a concerned party.

Decision in context

The complainant was a concerned party under Section 13(1). The Court held that failure to furnish the report violated that provision in the circumstances of the BSF proceedings, discussed Section 26 and directed BSF to pay the petitioner ₹25,000. It declined to revisit the punishment.

Supreme Court judgment on workplace misconduct and review of disciplinary findings

Supreme Court of India · December 2021 · Operative conclusion

The appeal is accordingly allowed

Decision in context

The Court set aside the Calcutta High Court decisions and dismissed the writ petition. It addressed the Commandant’s jurisdiction and whether the Summary Security Force Court had to give reasons under the then-applicable rules. It called for procedural and substantive fairness in workplace sexual-harassment cases.

Supreme Court judgment on safeguards in a judicial in-house inquiry

Supreme Court of India · December 2014 · Paragraph 46

The second stage of the “in-house procedure” is to be carried out, under the authority of the Chief Justice of India.

Decision in context

The High Court Chief Justice exceeded stage-one authority by constituting a two-judge committee for an in-depth probe. The Supreme Court directed safeguards against the judge’s administrative control over witnesses and left reinitiation of the in-house process to the Chief Justice of India.

Supreme Court judgment on transfer, involuntary resignation and reinstatement

Supreme Court of India · February 2022 · Paragraph 97

cannot be construed to be voluntary
thereby accepting the resignation of the petitioner, is quashed and set aside

Decision in context

The Court held the transfer and rejection of the representations unlawful on the facts, held the resignation involuntary, and directed reinstatement with continuity and consequential benefits, excluding back wages.

Supreme Court judgment on police investigation and courtroom safeguards

Supreme Court of India · August 2022 · Paragraphs 29 and 36–38

we direct that the investigation shall be supervised by a woman officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police

Decision in context

Directed police investigation where material evidence including CCTV footage was outside the complainant’s control. Discussed the Magistrate’s Section 156(3) CrPC discretion and safeguards for survivors in court.

Supreme Court order on hospital workplace safety and POSH compliance

Supreme Court of India · August 2024 · Paragraph 12(II)(a)–(b)

an Internal Complaints Committee must be constituted in all hospitals and nursing homes

Decision in context

The interim order identified POSH compliance in public and private hospitals and nursing homes as part of the National Task Force action-plan remit. It sought government-hospital data on committees and compliance. Cite it as an institutional direction within the safety proceedings.
